title: SQL Server Agent Jobs
description: Create, schedule, monitor, and troubleshoot SQL Server Agent jobs for backups, index maintenance, and ETL.

data.text: SQL Server Agent is the built-in scheduler. A job is a named container for one or more steps; a step is a T-SQL command, PowerShell script, SSIS package, or operating-system command; a schedule decides when the job runs. Job definitions, schedules, and history live in the `msdb` database, which is why backing up `msdb` matters as much as backing up user databases.

data.caption: A SQL Server Agent job is composed of ordered steps, triggered by one or more schedules, and records each run in msdb history.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    SCH["Schedule\ndaily at 02:00"] --> JOB["Job\nNightly Index Maintenance"]
    JOB --> S1["Step 1\nT-SQL maintenance"]
    S1 -->|success| S2["Step 2\nUpdate statistics"]
    S1 -->|failure| NOTIFY["Notify operator\nand retry"]
    S2 --> HIST["msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory"]
    NOTIFY --> HIST
    JOB --> TARGET["Target server(s)"]

data.text: The system procedures in `msdb` are the scriptable equivalent of SQL Server Management Studio's job editor. Create the job, add steps, create and attach a schedule, then add the job to a server. `@freq_type = 4` means daily and `@active_start_time = 020000` means 02:00:00 in HHMMSS form.

data.title: Create a nightly maintenance job
data.content: Retries are configured on the step, so a transient failure does not page anyone at 2 AM.

data.title: Show the last runs of every job
data.content: `step_id = 0` is the job outcome row. `run_status` uses 0 = failed, 1 = succeeded, 3 = canceled, 4 = in progress.
data.code:
SELECT
    j.name AS job_name,
    msdb.dbo.agent_datetime(h.run_date, h.run_time) AS run_at,
    h.run_status,
    h.run_duration
FROM msdb.dbo.sysjobs AS j
JOIN msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory AS h
    ON h.job_id = j.job_id
WHERE h.step_id = 0
ORDER BY h.run_date DESC, h.run_time DESC;

data.title: Agent jobs fail silently if nobody is watching
data.text: By default, a failed job just records a row in history. Configure an operator and a notification (email or net send) on failure, and set severity-based alerts for errors that matter. Also check that the SQL Server Agent service is running — when it is stopped, nothing fires and no one is told.

data.title: Make jobs idempotent and observable
data.text: A job that runs twice should not corrupt data or double-load a table. Write the step so it can be re-run safely, log start and end times to a table, and use `@retry_attempts` for transient failures. For long jobs, add a check that aborts if the previous run is still active rather than stacking executions.

data.title: Interview angle: Agent vs SQL Server Integration Services vs Azure Data Factory
data.text: SQL Server Agent is a scheduler, not an ETL engine. It can run T-SQL, PowerShell, and SSIS packages on a schedule, which is enough for backups, index maintenance, and small extracts. SSIS adds data-flow transformations and connectors. Azure Data Factory is the cloud-native orchestrator with triggers, linked services, and monitoring. A good answer separates scheduling from data movement instead of treating Agent as a full integration platform.

data.title: SQL Server Agent Jobs Key Points
points: A job contains ordered steps and runs on one or more schedules.
Job metadata and history live in msdb, so back up msdb regularly.
Use sp_add_job, sp_add_jobstep, sp_add_schedule, sp_attach_schedule, and sp_add_jobserver to script jobs.
Configure retries on steps and notifications on failure.
Query sysjobhistory with step_id = 0 to see job outcomes.
Agent schedules work; SSIS or Data Factory moves and transforms data.
